Basis: Civil Code article 138 (custodian of a thing, with the power of use, management and control, is liable for the harm the thing causes); the exemption paragraph (foreign cause: act of the victim, of a third party, unforeseeable event or force majeure).
Basis for animals: Civil Code article 139 (the custodian of an animal, even if it strayed or escaped, is liable unless he proves a foreign cause).

Basis for buildings: Civil Code article 140 (the owner of a building is liable for harm from its total or partial collapse unless he proves it was not due to lack of maintenance, age or a construction defect); the paragraph letting a threatened person demand preventive measures; the fire paragraph (holder of a building or movables where a fire started is liable only on proof of his fault).
Check whether product liability (Civil Code article 140 bis, producer of a defective product) is the better basis when the thing is a manufactured product.
Element: the defendant had custody (actual power of use, management and control) at the time of the harm; custody presumed in the owner but may be transferred (lessee, borrower, thief).
Element: the thing, animal or building intervened in causing the harm (active role) and the causal link to the harm.
Element: the harm itself (material and moral), its extent and its amount.

Burden of proof: the plaintiff proves custody, the intervention of the thing and the harm; no proof of fault is needed; the defendant bears proof of the foreign cause to escape (or, for a building, proof that the collapse was not due to lack of maintenance, age or defect).
Fault of the victim may reduce or exclude compensation (Civil Code article 177 on contributory fault of the creditor).
Several custodians or co-liable persons: joint and several liability (Civil Code article 126).

Compensation: assessment of tort damages by the judge (Civil Code article 131 referring to articles 182 and 182 bis), loss suffered and gain lost, moral damage (article 182 bis); form of compensation (article 132: money, instalments, income, or restoration).
Limitation: the tort action is barred after fifteen years from the day of the harmful act (Civil Code article 133); not raised by the court of its own motion, only on a plea (Civil Code article 321).
Interruption and suspension of the limitation (Civil Code articles 316-318: claim in court, acknowledgement); counting by days, first day not counted.
Where the harm results from an offence and the criminal action is not yet time-barred, check whether the civil claim survives as long as the public action (Code of Criminal Procedure article 10).
Formal notice: not required when the obligation is compensation arising from a harmful act (Civil Code article 181).
Section: civil section of the tribunal (Code of Civil Procedure article 32 on sections); if the court has no sections the case goes before the court as a whole.

Territory: general rule the defendant's domicile (Code of Civil Procedure article 37); in tort matters also the court where the harmful act occurred (Code of Civil Procedure article 39); not of public order for ordinary territorial rules.

Exit to administrative courts: when the custodian is the State, a wilaya, a commune or a public administrative body (Code of Civil Procedure articles 800-801), except damage caused by any vehicle belonging to them, which stays with the ordinary courts (article 802).

Exit to the criminal judge: the victim may bring the civil action before the criminal court seized of the offence; if a criminal action is pending on the same facts, the civil judge must stay (Code of Criminal Procedure article 4).
Exit to the specialised commercial court only for listed matters (maritime, air transport, insurance linked to commercial activity) — rarely applicable here.
Boundary: road traffic accidents with motor vehicles are governed by the special compensation regime of Ordinance 74-15 (insurer, fixed scales), not by article 138 alone.
Boundary: work accidents and occupational illnesses are covered by the social-security regime (Law 83-13) and its own litigation; not an ordinary custody claim against the employer.
Boundary: harm caused by a thing under a contract between the parties (e.g. lessor/lessee water leak, carrier) may fall under contractual liability; no cumulation of the two regimes.
Boundary: personal fault (Civil Code article 124) requires proof of fault; liability for others (articles 134-137) concerns persons, not things.
Boundary: neighbourhood nuisances beyond the usual (Civil Code article 691) are a different basis for a property owner.
Boundary: medical liability, product liability and liability for nuclear or environmental harm have special texts.
Prior steps: no compulsory conciliation; no formal notice; optional court-offered mediation (Code of Civil Procedure articles 990 ff. on conciliation, 994 ff. on mediation).
Petition formal elements: Code of Civil Procedure article 15 (court, parties, object, summary of facts and means, documents); standing and interest article 13; fees.

Documents: proof of harm (bailiff's report, expert report, photographs, medical certificates, invoices), proof of the custody (title, lease, registration of a vehicle or animal), police or gendarmerie report.

Accessory requests: expert appointment to assess harm; provisional execution (Code of Civil Procedure article 323 conditions); costs (article 419); interest is not due on tort compensation before judgment.
Insurance: the custodian's liability insurer may be joined; direct action of the victim against the insurer (Ordinance 95-07 on insurance).
Amendment memory: Civil Code amended by Law 05-10 of 20 June 2005 (added article 140 bis, 182 bis, changed 124 wording); article 138 itself not amended as far as I recall.
